public_rationale: OpenAI's 2025 statements show $7.5B cost of revenue and $5.73B sales and marketing on $13.07B revenue. The speaker says it is 'very clear' OpenAI moved numbers to look better, and he guesses that inference costs sit in S&M. Independent analysts at Epoch AI also guessed that free-user inference is in S&M. But that is an inference, and such a classification can be a defensible accounting choice. I found no filing, auditor note, restatement, company statement or reputable report that documents how OpenAI books inference. I also found nothing reconciling the Azure inference figures with cost of revenue. OpenAI's IPO filing is still confidential. The evidence neither shows numbers were moved to flatter results nor rules it out.
limitations: The techstrong article's exact publication date is not shown on the page. It appeared after the mid-June 2026 leak.
Whether a policy of booking free-user inference as S&M counts as 'moving numbers' is a judgment the evidence cannot make.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: It is very clear that OpenAI moved numbers around to make things look better than they are, and he believes its inference costs are being booked under sales and marketing.

statement.excerpt: It’s very clear OpenAI moved around numbers to make things look better than they are, and I believe that inference costs are being dumped in sales and marketing.

from_speaker: It's very clear OpenAI moved around numbers to make things look better than they are
I believe that inference costs are being dumped in sales and marketing
$7.5 billion cost of revenue on $13.07 billion in revenue
$8.67 billion on inference in the first nine months of 2025
our_interpretation: The firm claim is that OpenAI presented its 2025 costs so that results looked better than the underlying economics. For example, it put some costs outside cost of revenue, flattering gross margin, or shifted figures between line items.

The 'I believe' clause about inference sitting in sales and marketing is the speaker's own hedged guess. It is not required for support. Evidence that inference costs were booked in S&M or another non-cost-of-revenue line would count toward the firm claim. So would any other documented reclassification.
Target period: OpenAI's 2025 financial statements, which are the numbers he discusses.
criteria.support_condition: A credible source documents that OpenAI classified or shifted costs, such as inference compute, outside cost of revenue in a way that makes its 2025 margins or losses look better. Sources could be a public filing, auditor notes, a restatement, an OpenAI statement, or reputable reporting on its accounting.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A credible source shows OpenAI's 2025 inference compute was fully in cost of revenue under consistent policies. Or a source explains the gap between the roughly $8.67B nine-month Azure inference figure and the $7.5B full-year cost of revenue without any flattering reclassification.

evidence.excerpt: Cost of revenue rose to $7.5 billion from $2.65 billion, reflecting substantial infrastructure and computing costs incurred at inference time as user prompts scaled. Sales and marketing, meanwhile, expanded fivefold, from $1.11 billion to $5.73 billion
evidence.explanation: Confirms the 2025 line items the speaker discusses. It says nothing about how costs were classified or whether anything was moved.

evidence.excerpt: Our explanation of the discrepancy is that the 2025 H1 S&M spending includes the cost of inference for free users, OpenAI’s primary way of advertising their products, while the 2024 figure does not.
evidence.explanation: Independent analysts also suspect free-user inference sits in S&M. That is consistent with the speaker's hedged guess. But it is their inference, not a disclosure, and it does not show numbers were moved to mislead.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A public S-1 or audited statements with notes showing where OpenAI books inference compute for paid and free users. Or reputable reporting or an OpenAI statement documenting any reclassification, or explaining the gap between its inference spend and cost of revenue.
